samples.text:
In many big cities, people live very close to each other but they do not know even the names of their neighbours. This essay will explain why this is happening and how cities can build a stronger community.

There are a few reasons for this problem. Firstly, people in cities are very busy with their work. They leave home early in the morning and come back late at night, so they have no time for talking with neighbours. Secondly, many people live in big apartment buildings where hundreds of families live, and it is difficult to know everybody. Also, people in cities often move house because of their job or rent, so they do not stay in one place for long time. Finally, technology is another reason. People spend their free time on their phones and social media instead of go outside and meet the people near them.

However, there are some ways to make a stronger community in cities. The local government can organise events like street festivals or sports competitions where neighbours can meet each other. For example, in some cities there are markets at weekends where people from the same area come together. Another idea is to build more parks and community centres, because these places give people chance to talk and make friends. Also, apartment buildings could create online groups for residents so they can share informations and help each other.

In conclusion, people in cities do not know their neighbours because they are busy, they move often and they use technology too much. I believe that events and public spaces can help to create stronger community, but people also need to make an effort themselves.
samples.why: Answers both questions with relevant causes and solutions · ideas general and list-like · repetitive linking (Also, Firstly) · adequate vocabulary · errors in word order, articles and countability that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
It is often said that city dwellers can live next door to someone for years without ever having a conversation with them. This essay will consider the main reasons for this lack of connection and suggest how urban communities could be strengthened.

The primary cause is the pace of urban life. Long working hours and lengthy commutes mean that many residents spend little time in their neighbourhood apart from sleeping there, leaving few opportunities for casual encounters. The design of modern housing makes the situation worse. In large apartment blocks, residents typically move directly from a car park or lift to their own front door, and there are rarely shared spaces where people might naturally stop and chat. Furthermore, city populations are highly mobile. Young professionals in particular tend to rent for a year or two before moving on, so there is little incentive to invest time in getting to know the people around them.

Despite these obstacles, a stronger sense of community can be encouraged. Urban planners have an important role to play by including communal areas such as small parks, playgrounds and shared gardens in new developments, since these places allow relationships to form gradually through repeated contact. Local councils could also support neighbourhood events, for instance by closing a street for an afternoon so that residents can hold a party or a market. On a smaller scale, digital tools can be helpful when they are used to connect people locally; neighbourhood messaging groups allow residents to lend tools, share recommendations and organise activities, which often leads to face-to-face friendship.

In conclusion, urban residents rarely know their neighbours because of busy lifestyles, isolating building design and frequent relocation. These problems can be reduced through better planning, local events and the sensible use of technology, although individuals also need to be willing to make first move.
samples.why: Both questions answered with clearly extended causes and solutions · logical organisation with clear topic sentences · good collocation (lengthy commutes, casual encounters) · mostly accurate complex sentences with one article slip.

samples.text:
Paradoxically, cities pack people together more densely than anywhere else, yet many urban residents could not name the person living on the other side of their wall. This anonymity has social, economic and architectural roots, but it is not inevitable, and there are practical ways in which a sense of community can be rebuilt.

One fundamental reason is the structure of urban working life. Long hours and extended commutes turn many homes into little more than places to sleep, so residents are seldom around at the times when neighbourly contact might occur. Transience compounds the problem. In cities where a large proportion of people rent, tenants may move every year or two, and there is little motivation to build relationships that seem likely to be short-lived. Architecture also plays a part: high-rise blocks with anonymous corridors and underground parking allow people to travel from their car to their flat without encountering anyone. Finally, online social networks now satisfy much of the need for connection that was once met locally, making it easy to feel sociable while remaining a stranger to one's neighbours.

Rebuilding community therefore requires action on several levels. Planners can design spaces that encourage chance encounters, such as courtyards, shared gardens and pedestrian-friendly streets lined with small shops and cafés, since relationships tend to grow out of repeated informal contact rather than organised gatherings. Local authorities can supplement this by funding regular events, from street parties to volunteering schemes, which give residents a shared purpose. Technology, too, can be turned to advantage; neighbourhood apps that allow people to borrow items or offer help frequently lead to offline friendships. Longer tenancy agreements would also help, giving renters the stability needed to put down roots.

In conclusion, city dwellers remain strangers because of demanding schedules, frequent relocation, isolating architecture and online distractions. Thoughtful urban design, community events and local digital networks, supported by more secure housing, can go a long way towards restoring neighbourly ties.
samples.why: Both questions fully developed with causes explicitly linked to solutions · skilful cohesion and paragraphing · wide, precise vocabulary (transience, compounds, put down roots) · varied complex structures, essentially error-free.
